newsitem.title: USA: CFTC enforcement arm issues "substantial" fines.
newsitem.headline: CFTC enforcement arm issues "substantial" fines.

text.p: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission imposed what it described as "substantial" fines in a wash trading settlement with Mitsubishi Corp and Merrill Lynch Futures Inc, a senior CFTC official said Tuesday.

"These amounts will be viewed as pretty substantial by the industry," Geoffrey Aronow, the head of the CFTC's enforcement division, said in an interview. "It's important that the message be there that the commission is prepared to aggressively enforce regulations."
Earlier on Tuesday, the agency said Merrill agreed to pay $175,000, Mitsubishi $150,000 and Country Hedging Inc $75,000 as part of an agreement settling charges of wash trading in wheat futures.
The Minnesota Grain Exchange brought the matter to the CFTC's attention after spotting suspected wash sales.

Agency investigators analyzed trading cards, computer data and other records and eventually determined that Mitsubishi tried to shift futures trading profits from one reporting period to another for accounting purposes.
The firm placed simultaneous orders with its brokerage firm, Merrill Lynch, to buy and sell equal quantities of wheat futures at the same price.
"In a wash sale, you can't measure direct harm to someone. This is injury to the integrity of the marketplace," Aronow said.
The case was the latest in the agency's stepped-up pace of enforcement activity.
On Monday, the CFTC said it had won a federal court order freezing the assets of a California telemarketing company accused of selling illegal off-exchange precious metals futures contracts.

In a lawsuit filed last Wednesday, the CFTC accused Golden State Bullion, its president and three telemarketing employees with making high-pressure sales pitches for risky investments in platinum, gold, silver and palladium. The firm allegedly wooed investors by promising that impending labor trouble at South African mines would cause platium prices to soar to nearly $700 per ounce.
"Telemarketing is a continuing area of concern to the commission," Aronow said. "These cases are about the use of telemarketing devices to try and defraud people."
